newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian banking needs Euro-size player - banker.
newsitem.headline: Belgian banking needs Euro-size player - banker.

text.p: The Belgian banking scene needs to see mergers between its larger players to create a European-sized bank which can compete with Europe's majors, the chief executive officer of Paribas Bank Belgium said on Wednesday.

"The fragmentation of the banking scene is a serious handicap. Belgium needs a couple of large financial institutions which can play a significant role on a European level," Philippe Romagnoli told a news conference on the bank's 1996 results.
"The project of a Grande Banque Belge will resurface."

Speculation on the creation of a Grande Banque Belge was rife about a year ago, driving the share prices of top Belgian banks higher, but it died a death after some of the shareholders involved voiced their opposition to certain merger scenarios.
At the time the merger talk focused on Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL), Gemeentekrediet van Belgie/Credit Communal de Belgique (CCB) and Generale Bank.
CCB has since teamed up with Credit Local de France, but in terms of joint assets estimated at some $970 billion, it is still only number 22 in Europe.

Romagnoli said it would desirable for at least two, if not three, of the major banks in Belgium to merge to create an institution with a balance total of at least 15,000 billion Belgian francs or $500 billion.
The Belgian banking market is currently dominated by the so-called Seven Sisters: BBL, Generale Bank, Kredietbank -- all listed -- and Bacob Bank, Cera Bank, Gemeentekrediet and ASLK/CGER.
The largest, Generale Bank, has a balance sheet total of about 4,040 billion francs. It would take a merger of at least the top five to create a bank of the size Romagnoli envisages.

Alternatively, Belgian banks could look abroad. There are plenty of large domestic players in neighbouring countries looking to achieve a European size as well before the start of the European Union's single currency union.
Economic and monetary union in the EU will boost competition, while removing the ability for banks to resort to their own currency area and home market.

"It opens European perspectives for those wishing to cover a larger area than Belgium and its immediate neighbours either as a niche player or a comprehensive commercial bank. Prima facia, Belgian banks are not ready for this," Romagnoli said.
"Attitudes are still oriented towards one's own region."

Paribas Bank Belgium, 63.22 percent owned by Paribas International, part of French Banque Paribas, and 14.21 percent by Belgian holding company Cobepa, would, however, not be part of the expected concentration drive, he added.
